claims.statement: Battery producers and producer-responsibility organisations have a recurring statutory need and budget for collection, treatment and recycling, and select permitted waste-management operators.
EU recycling and material-recovery targets create recurring documentation and quality obligations around accepted treatment.
The current EU bottleneck is not generic recycler-capacity scarcity: the Commission says relevant capacity is largely under-used and recyclers need black-mass feedstock.
Cross-border waste routing can require notification, consent, an effective contract and financial assurance, and new hazardous battery-waste classifications increase compliance sensitivity.
Recircle.market and ReBattery are direct product substitutes for marketplace discovery, battery-data exchange, recycler matching, quotes and documentation.
Large industrial actors can secure feedstock and refining through bilateral purchase agreements rather than open capacity booking.
A single-corridor compliant routing service may still reduce fragmented matching and documentation work, but it is more plausibly a feedstock-routing service than a forward capacity exchange.
Customers will pay 20-50 PLN per reserved tonne or route 50000 tonnes per year through a new entrant.
A prototype is founder-compatible, but anchor acquisition and regulated cross-border execution are unlikely to remain a 2-4-hour-per-day solo activity without delegated specialists.

contrary_evidence: The Commission directly reports largely under-used capacity and a feedstock shortage.
Two visible platforms already overlap the marketplace and recycler-routing proposition.
A major recycling chain uses a bilateral purchase agreement, suggesting counterparties may prefer closed contracts.
Waste-shipment approvals and financial assurance prevent a simple software booking from completing many cross-border routes.
